title: My family
goal: Name family members, use possessives that follow the noun's group, and ask someone's age.
bekal: tell *hans*, *hendes* and *sin* apart — the most famous trap in Danish
wave: Go back over **Unit 3** first: point at ten things around you, name each with its *en* or *et*, then change it into the form with the ending.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Billeder på telefonen
dialogs.intro: Mette shows Budi photos of her family.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Se her — det er min familie.
lines.literal: see here — it is my family.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Who's the man with the beard?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Det er min far. Han hedder Jens.
lines.id: That's my dad. His name is Jens.
lines.literal: it is my father. he is-called Jens.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And the woman next to him?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Det er min mor, Anne. Og det er mine to brødre.
lines.id: That's my mom, Anne. And those are my two brothers.
lines.literal: it is my mother, Anne. and it is my two brothers.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Lars er nitten, og Peter er fjorten. Jeg er den ældste.
lines.id: Lars is nineteen, and Peter is fourteen. I'm the oldest.
lines.literal: Lars is nineteen, and Peter is fourteen. I am the oldest.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do you have a sister too?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Nej. Men min bror har en kæreste — hende der.
lines.id: No. But my brother has a girlfriend — that one there.
lines.literal: no. but my brother has a sweetheart — her there.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Ja, i hendes lejlighed i Aarhus. Han elsker sin cykel mere end hende.
lines.id: Yes, in her apartment in Aarhus. He loves his bike more than her.
lines.literal: yes, in her apartment in Aarhus. he loves his-own bike more than her.

notes: **The possessive follows the noun, not the owner.** *Min far* but *mit hus* — and what decides it isn't who owns it, but whether *far* and *hus* are en-words or et-words. English has just one *my*; Danish has three.
**Ved siden af** = "next to". Literally "by the side of". Danish place expressions are often three-word chunks like this; learn them whole, don't take them apart.
**Hvor gamle er de?** Note *gamle*, not *gammel* — since you're asking about more than one person, the adjective ends in *-e*. For one person: *Hvor gammel er du?*
**Age without an extra verb.** *Jeg er femogtyve* is enough; you can also say it in full: *jeg er femogtyve år gammel*. Danish uses *er* like English (*I am 25*), not *har* like French or Spanish.
**Den ældste** = "the oldest". The forms are irregular: *gammel → ældre → ældst* — like English *old → elder → eldest*. Notice the double definite again: *den* in front, *-e* on the adjective.

**Sin cykel — here's the trap.** *Han elsker **sin** cykel* = he loves **his own** bike. If you write *han elsker **hans** cykel*, it means he loves **another man's** bike. English "his" can mean either; Danish must make the difference.
**En kæreste** is used for a boyfriend or a girlfriend — Danish doesn't distinguish. Literally "dearest". For married couples: *en mand* (husband) and *en kone* (wife).

grammars.title: Possessives
body: Only the first three rows change form. The rest have one form for everything — an unexpected relief.

head: Owner
en-word
et-word
Plural
Example
rows: min far, mit hus, mine bøger
din mor, dit værelse, dine nøgler
hans bil, hans hus, hans børn

after: *Hans*, *hendes*, *vores*, *jeres*, *deres* never change, whatever the noun. Only *min/din/sin* and their forms need attention.

Danish also has a possessive **-s**, just like English but without the apostrophe: *Mettes far* (Mette's dad), *Danmarks hovedstad* (Denmark's capital), *min brors cykel* (my brother's bike). It's the most common form with people's names.

grammars.title: Sin, hans or hendes?
body: The only rule you need to remember: **sin/sit/sine is used when the owner is the subject of that same sentence.** Otherwise, use *hans* or *hendes*.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: His mother calls Peter. (*sin* is impossible here)

after: The last row shows the fence on the other side: **sin can never be part of the subject**. If the possessive stands in front of the verb as part of the subject, it must be *hans* or *hendes*.
The same goes for the plural: *De tager **deres** cykler* — but even when they mean their own, modern Danish still uses *deres*. So in practice this trap only applies to the third person singular.
This mistake won't make you misunderstood, but it marks you as a beginner instantly. Getting it right, on the other hand, is one of the quickest signs that someone is learning seriously.

blocks.text: *Brødre* (plural of *bror*) and *søstre* (plural of *søster*) change form. To talk about brothers and sisters together, Danish has one very handy everyday word: **søskende** — "siblings", but far more common than the English word.
Step-relatives are formed with the prefix *sted-*: *en stedfar*, *en stedmor*, *en stedsøster*. Modern Danish families are often complicated, and these words are used without any awkwardness.

*At fylde* literally means "to fill" — *at fylde tredive* = to turn thirty. *En fødselsdag* literally means "birth day", built from *fødsel* + *dag*. Danish loves gluing words into one long word; if you meet a word that looks impossible, try breaking it up first.

blocks.title: Compound words: the key to reading Danish
items: ⚠️ A compound's group is always decided by **the last word**: *et skab* → *et køleskab*. It's the only truly reliable rule for guessing a word's group.

exercises.prompt: Fill in min, mit or mine.

items: Mette ringer til ____ mor. (her own mother)
____ far er lærer. (Peter's father, as subject)
I have two brothers and one sister.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: min — mit — mine — mit — min — mine
Det er min familie. — Hvor gammel er du? — Jeg er femogtyve år gammel. — Jeg har to brødre og en søster. — Hvem er kvinden? — Hun ringer til sin mor.
Det er min familie. — Hvor gammel er du? — Jeg har to brødre. — Han tager sin cykel. — De bor i hendes lejlighed.
